claims.text: Rapid, recurrent formation of a stable, multielement-enriched passive oxide film is the dominant factor governing enhanced tribocorrosion resistance in high-entropy alloys.
The passive oxide film reforms after being locally damaged by sliding.
Reformation of the passive film limits surface degradation, material loss, and accelerated corrosion at wear sites.
AlCrTiZrMo provides multiple oxide-forming elements suitable for producing a protective multicomponent oxide.
Standard melting and annealing can produce the proposed test alloy with a homogeneous and uniform solid-solution microstructure.
High configurational entropy can favor single-phase solid-solution formation in HEAs.
A transient multicomponent oxide layer forms and reforms during sliding-induced degradation.
The transient oxide layer maintains a protective barrier against both mechanical wear and electrochemical attack.
A dense ZrTiO4 surface oxide on annealed AlCrTiZrMo can prevent continued oxidation.
Re-establishment of a coherent oxide barrier after abrasion reduces the synergistic acceleration between wear damage and corrosion.
The proposed film-regeneration mechanism mitigates wear and corrosion simultaneously.
The HEA will have significantly lower combined tribocorrosion mass loss than the conventional-alloy baseline.
The HEA will have a lower friction coefficient than the baseline.
The HEA will have a lower corrosion current density than the baseline.
Electrochemical impedance will indicate a more stable passive film over repeated wear cycles in the HEA than in the baseline.
A conventional baseline such as 304L regenerates its passive film less efficiently and consequently has a higher tribocorrosion rate.
The protective effect should operate at moderate contact loads and typical chloride concentrations.
Sufficiently high stress, temperature, or chloride concentration can make film removal or breakdown exceed the alloy's capacity to repassivate.
